flow.d: Receiving and shipping share the south wall, so one yard, one gatehouse and one set of dock equipment serve both.
The busiest SKUs sit in the front bays, close to packing and to receiving, so both their picks and their put-aways are short.
C items fill the far end of the aisles, where few trips go.

flow.t: In and out side by side
flow.d: Receiving and shipping lanes sit next to each other: trucks and staging have to be kept apart by markings and door rules.

flow.t: Room to grow away from the dock
flow.d: The building can be extended north without moving a door.

flow.t: In one side, out the other
flow.d: Receiving on the west wall, shipping on the east wall: goods move one way through the building.

flow.t: Fast movers at the shipping end
flow.d: The busiest SKUs sit at the east ends of the aisles, next to packing, so picks stay short.
The forklift carries every fast-mover pallet the full length of the building, from the receiving side to the shipping end.
Receiving and packing are on opposite sides, but the forklift still carries fast-mover pallets to the east end, where the pickers work.
Trucks need a yard on both sides of the building: more paving, two gates and two sets of dock staff or a walk across the building.

flow.t: In on one wall, out on the next
flow.d: Receiving on the south wall, shipping on the east wall: goods turn one corner on the way through.
The busiest SKUs sit in the front bays at the east end, close to packing and to the receiving doors near the corner.
Inbound trucks use the south yard and outbound trucks the east yard. Their lanes meet beyond the corner, so the site needs room and traffic rules there.
With the doors near the corner, the south-west of the dock zone is free for value-added work, returns or more staging.
The north and west walls stay free to extend the building.
